extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Expository guidance on measuring and awarding damages, interest, costs, nominal awards, trebling, distribution, and evidentiary burdens in U.S. patent-infringement actions. Focused on when different measures (royalty/license fee, value of use, profits) apply and procedural/equitable adjustments courts may make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of actual damages: license fee, value of use, or defendant's profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual damages may be measured by an established license fee (royalty), by the value of the use of the invention to the defendant, or by the profits on the defendant's sales. Recovery of profits or value is generally limited to acts performed before the suit was instituted; subsequent similar acts are new injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a license fee has been adopted, the patentee is generally entitled to recover that fee (covering the entire value as fixed by the patentee). Recovery of profits for use of a machine ordinarily covers only the period prior to recovery and does not vest title in the defendant. Cases cited: Spaulding v. Page; Sawyer; Sickels v. Borden; Stone Cutter Co. v. Sheldons. When the measure is profits or value to defendant, interest computation differs (see Interest rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of judgment/payment on future use and on purchasers (vendees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction of a judgment (payment of damages) does not authorize any future use or sale of the invention; paying a judgment does not grant the defendant a right to repeat the infringing acts. Buyers of infringing articles (vendees) have an implied license to use purchased articles until they are destroyed, but neither judgment nor its payment authorizes repetition of the infringing acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff who sells licenses may preserve exclusivity; where patentee has received compensation for sale of a specific machine embodying the invention that specific machine may be freed from monopoly (Bloomer v. Millinger). Settlement by vendor with patentee for past infringements does not protect subsequent vendees (Matthews v. Spangenberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of damages and new injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages awarded are estimated in view of acts performed before the suit; any subsequent acts of the same character constitute new injuries requiring separate redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery of established patent fee may cover entire term if properly fixed by patentee; recovery of profits is usually only for the limited period prior to suit. Courts treat later infringements as separate causes of action and not barred by earlier judgments for past infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on damages: when recoverable and computation start date
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance of interest on items composing actual damages depends on the chosen measure of damages. For license fees (royalties) interest is computed from the date the royalty should have been paid in the usual course of business. For damages measured by value of use or by profits, interest runs from the date the defendant received the benefit or profits. For damages measured by the plaintiff's diminished sales or prices (injury to plaintiff's enjoyment), interest begins at the date of suit. Interest continues to the date of judgment and should be included in the award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where royalties are the measure, interest from royalty due-date (Creamer v. Bowers). Where loss is measured by plaintiff's diminished sales, interest commences at suit date. Where damages are unliquidated until verdict (e.g., profits-based), the date may vary. Cases: National Car Brake Shoe Co. v. Terre Haute Car & Mfg. Co.; Bates v. St. Johnsbury & L. C. R. R. Co.; May v. County of Fond du Lac. Equity practice and discretion of court may affect interest allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel fees and litigation expenses are not elements of actual damages (but equitable relief/costs may differ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel fees and other litigation expenses generally do not enter into actual damages; they are exceptions and may be allowed as taxable costs in some equitable contexts or where legally chargeable to the defendant. The court's power to increase damages in certain cases enables protection against wanton or unreasonable defiance and may serve to punish the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors are required to find actual damages incurred at time suit was brought and not include counsel fees. In equity, allowance of interest and some costs is largely discretionary. Cases: Parks v. Booth; Teese v. Huntingdon; related discussion at §1162.

rubrics_metrics.name: When only nominal damages are recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominal damages are the only recovery when the plaintiff fails to prove an established license fee or depreciation in value of exclusive use, or when the proof does not establish a proper measure of actual damages. Nominal damages are also proper in several specific situations enumerated by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations giving rise to only nominal damages include: (a) plaintiff claims a close monopoly but did not preserve it and no license fee is proved (Burdell v. Denig); (b) open, cheap, and equally useful methods exist and no license fee proved; (c) only certain claims of little importance were infringed; (d) only the making of an article without sale or use; (e) plaintiff misled defendant; (f) plaintiff's device not stamped or due notice not given; (g) only one claim valid and no license fee proven. Juries cannot lawfully award more than nominal damages where evidence supports only nominal damages — such a verdict is fatal and requires new trial. Cases: Blake v. Greenwood Cemetery; Carter v. Baker; Whittemore v. Cutter; McComb v. Brodie; Johnson v. Boot; others cited in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's statutory discretion to increase (treble) damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may increase a jury's award of actual damages to an amount not exceeding three times the verdict. This is a judicial (not jury) power, used primarily in cases of wanton infringement or where the defendant compelled the plaintiff to needlessly expensive litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trebling is discretionary and applied to punish malicious or persistent infringers, to remunerate patentees forced into protracted litigation, and where the verdict alone would be inadequate. The court should confine jury verdicts to actual damages and then, if appropriate, treble them. Factors reducing or negating trebling include good faith belief in right, acting under protection of a rival patent, or bona fide purchaser/assignee-for-speculation status of plaintiff. Cases: Russell v. Place; Judson v. Bradford; Brodie v. Ophir Silver Mining Co.; Bell v. McCullough; Schwarzel v. Holenshade. Trebling may be inappropriate where defendant reasonably believed in the validity of its rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of recovered damages among multiple plaintiffs and owners
rubrics_metrics.description: When several plaintiffs are entitled to portions of recovered damages, the verdict need not specify shares; the total may be awarded in gross and distributed among plaintiffs according to their respective interests. Part owners suing each other recover only the portion commensurate with their interest. Damages recovered by an executor belong to the estate if infringement occurred during testator's life, otherwise to equitable owners represented by the executor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may order payment into court or execution and apportion among claimants. In suits by joint plaintiffs or multiple owners, recovery is proportional to interest. Cases: Campbell v. James; Goodyear v. Providence Rubber Co.; Herring v. Gas Consumers Association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and evidentiary requirements for damages and profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proving existence and amount of damages rests on the plaintiff, who must produce sufficient evidence and the necessary data to satisfy the jury and enable computation. To recover profits, plaintiff must show the amount of profits made by the defendant from the infringement and what portion is attributable to the patented invention; absent such proof only nominal damages may be awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must provide concrete data and calculations (not speculative guesses). Evidence is to be interpreted liberally in favor of the plaintiff, especially where infringement was wilful. Where defendant concealed profits, and plaintiff adduces available evidence, courts may permit recovery. Plaintiff need not exclude every other possible hypothetical cause once he shows infringement caused his loss and rebuts defendant's contributory cause suggestions. Cases: Rude v. Westcott; Tuttle v. Gaylord; Tilghman v. Proctor; Creamer v. Bowers; Dobson v. Dorman; Bigelow Carpet Co. v. Dobson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of proof at trial in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: After the general issue is closed, the plaintiff proceeds first and must introduce evidence to make out a prima facie case on the averments of the declaration. The letters-patent or certified copy are part of the plaintiff's evidentiary foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must present the evidence required to make a prima facie case; if he rests after merely proving infringement without the data to compute damages, he may be limited to nominal damages. The defendant's evidentiary objections and admissibility issues do not excuse plaintiff's burden to put forward substantial proof of damages or profits. Cases: National Car Brake Shoe Co.; Ganetson v. Clark; other trial procedure references.
